# Working environment {#sec-m1-ambiente}

## What to install

There are three components, in this order:

1. **R**: the language itself. <https://cran.r-project.org/>. Install the latest version
   (4.4 or later).
2. **RStudio Desktop**: the development environment. <https://posit.co/downloads/>.
3. **Rtools** (Windows only): build tools, needed to install
   packages that must be compiled from source, such as `sf` and `terra`:
   <https://cran.r-project.org/bin/windows/Rtools/>. Pick the version that matches your
   R version.

::: {.callout-important}
## Installing on an institutional machine

On Ministry computers, R and RStudio usually have to be installed by the IT
team. In the same ticket, it is worth asking for: (i) R and RStudio, (ii) Rtools, (iii) write permission on
a user package library folder and (iv) access to `cran.r-project.org`,
`github.com` and the data domains (`servicodados.ibge.gov.br`, `apiservice.mdic.gov.br`,
`web3.antaq.gov.br`). Without item (iv), installing packages and *downloading* data fail.
:::

Check the installation in the RStudio console:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
R.version.string
#> [1] "R version 4.6.0 (2026-04-24 ucrt)"
```
:::


## Always work inside a project

An **RStudio project** is a folder with an `.Rproj` file. It sets the *working
directory*, which makes relative paths stable. Go to `File > New Project > New Directory`.

Recommended structure:

```
meu-projeto/
├── meu-projeto.Rproj
├── dados/            # input data (never edited by hand)
│   └── brutos/       # raw data
├── R/                # scripts
│   ├── 01-leitura.R
│   ├── 02-limpeza.R
│   └── 03-analise.R
├── resultados/       # tables and charts produced
└── relatorios/       # reports: .qmd / .Rmd
```

Three rules that avoid most reproducibility problems:

1. **Never** use `setwd("C:/Users/...")`. Use the project and relative paths.
2. **Never** edit raw data. Cleaning is done in code, so that it can be audited and
   redone when the data are updated.
3. Turn off automatic restoring of `.RData` in
   `Tools > Global Options > General`, unticking *Restore .RData into workspace at startup*
   and choosing *Never* in *Save workspace*. That way your session always starts clean and you
   find out early if the script depends on something that is not written in it.

To build paths across operating systems, use `file.path()`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
file.path("dados", "cabotagem_tku_2025.csv")
#> [1] "dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.csv"
```
:::


## How to organise the course scripts

This material's recommendation is simple and worth following to the letter: **one R script per
module**, inside your project. When you open Module 2, create `R/modulo2.R` (or
`modulo2.qmd`) and paste the code blocks from this site into it, in order. Each module is
**independent**: the Module 2 script does not expect the Module 1 script to have run first, and
Module 3 does not depend on Module 2. This is on purpose, not a limitation:

- Each chapter downloads and stores in `dados/brutos/` (or reads from `dados/`) everything it needs, so
  running a module's script from start to finish, in a fresh R session, always works.
- You can revisit Module 2 weeks later without re-running earlier modules
  to "rebuild the state" of the session.
- Copy-and-paste mistakes stay contained in a single script instead of spreading to the
  rest of the course.

```
meu-projeto/
├── meu-projeto.Rproj
├── dados/
│   └── brutos/
├── R/
│   ├── modulo1.R      # everything you run in Module 1, top to bottom
│   ├── modulo2.R      # starts from scratch: library(sf), reading the data, etc.
│   └── modulo3.R
└── resultados/
```

The only care really needed: start each script in a clean session (the tip in the previous
section, about turning off automatic `.RData` restore, exists exactly for this) and
with the `library()`/`::` calls from the start of the chapter. If a block fails because an object "does not
exist", it is almost always because an earlier chunk of the **same** module has not been pasted or
run yet.

## Packages


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("dplyr")      # installs (once)
library(dplyr)                 # loads (in each session)
dplyr::filter                  # uses without loading
packageVersion("dplyr")        # installed version
update.packages(ask = FALSE)   # updates everything
```
:::


CRAN packages are installed with `install.packages()`. Development versions on GitHub are
installed differently. This is common for transport packages such as `flownet`:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("SebKrantz/flownet")
```
:::


::: {.callout-tip}
## Record the versions

At the end of a script or report, `sessionInfo()` (or `sessioninfo::session_info()`)
prints the R version and the version of every loaded package. Pasting that output into the annex of a
technical report is what makes it possible to reproduce the result months later.
:::

## Lock versions with `renv`

`sessionInfo()` **records** the versions. `renv` goes further: it **reproduces** the environment.
Each project gets its own package library, isolated from the others, and a
`renv.lock` file listing the exact version of each package used.

The problem it solves is concrete. You deliver a technical note in 2026 with a script
that runs. In 2028 someone needs to update the numbers, opens the script, and it fails: `sf`
changed an argument, `dplyr` deprecated a function. Without `renv`, nobody knows any more which
versions produced that result.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("renv")

renv::init()       # once, at the start of the project: creates the library and renv.lock
renv::snapshot()   # after installing or updating packages: writes the versions to the lock
renv::status()     # is the lock consistent with what the code uses?
renv::restore()    # on someone else's machine (or yours, two years from now)
```
:::


The workflow, in practice:

1. Create the project and run `renv::init()`.
2. Install packages as usual, with `install.packages()`.
3. When the script works, run `renv::snapshot()`.
4. Put `renv.lock` under version control together with the code (Git and GitHub, in Module 5). **Do not** version the
   `renv/library/` folder, which is large and which `renv` itself already adds to `.gitignore`.

Whoever receives the project runs a single command, `renv::restore()`, and gets exactly the same
versions.

::: {.callout-note}
## `renv` on an institutional machine

`renv` keeps a global package *cache*, so the same version of `sf` is not downloaded
again for each project. On computers behind a proxy, `restore()` depends on the same access to CRAN
as `install.packages()`; if one fails, so does the other. Sort out access first.
:::

## Where to look for help


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
?mean                      # function documentation
help(package = "dplyr")    # package documentation
vignette(package = "sf")   # long tutorials of the package
example(mean)              # runnable examples
```
:::


A package's documentation usually also has a *website*, easier to read, with usage articles:
`sf`, `dplyr`, `r5r` and `geobr` are good examples.

## AI in the workflow

AI assistants speed up R work a lot, especially in three situations:

- **Turning intent into code**: "group by destination state and sum the TKU" becomes `dplyr`
  code in seconds.
- **Interpreting error messages**: pasting the message and the surrounding lines usually gives the
  diagnosis right away.
- **Converting routines**: turning a procedure done in ArcGIS/QGIS, or a spreadsheet
  with formulas, into an equivalent script.

Ways to use them inside RStudio or VS Code:

| Tool | How it fits the workflow |
|:--|:--|
| GitHub Copilot | Autocomplete inside RStudio (`Tools > Global Options > Copilot`) |
| Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini (browser) | Paste code/error and ask for an explanation or review |
| `ellmer` package | Call models from inside R, within a script |
| `chattr`, `gander` | *Chat* interface attached to RStudio |

### What you **cannot** paste

Any text pasted into an AI assistant hosted outside the organisation leaves the Ministry's network. In
services for personal use, it may also be used to train future models. The rule is
simple: **if you would not publish the content on the Ministry's website, do not paste it.**

In our context, this includes:

- Spreadsheets from ongoing studies, drafts of technical notes, terms of reference.
- Any personal data (name, CPF tax number, licence plate, an individual's address), which is also
  covered by Brazil's data protection law (LGPD).
- Credentials: passwords, API *tokens*, database connection *strings*. A *token*
  pasted once must be considered leaked.

### How to ask for help without pasting the data

Most of the time the AI does not need your data. It needs its **structure** and the
**error**. Three safe ways, from the simplest to the most complete:

**1. Describe the format.** Instead of pasting the table:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
str(links)        # paste the OUTPUT of this: column names and types, without the content
names(links)
```
:::


**2. Build a toy dataset** with the same structure and made-up values:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
exemplo <- data.frame(
  no        = c(1, 1, 2),
  sentido   = c("direto", "inverso", "direto"),
  volvehprt = c(100, 80, 250),
  comprimento_km = c(0.5, 0.5, 1.2)
)
dput(exemplo)     # paste the output: it is text and recreates the table instantly
#> structure(list(no = c(1, 1, 2), sentido = c("direto", "inverso", 
#> "direto"), volvehprt = c(100, 80, 250), comprimento_km = c(0.5, 
#> 0.5, 1.2)), class = "data.frame", row.names = c(NA, -3L))
```
:::


**3. Make a minimal reproducible example with `reprex`.** It runs your snippet in a clean
session and formats code and output ready to paste into a *chat*, a forum or an *issue*:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
install.packages("reprex")

reprex::reprex({
  exemplo <- data.frame(no = c(1, 1, 2), volvehprt = c(100, 80, 250))
  exemplo |> dplyr::summarise(total = sum(volvehprt), .by = no)
})
```
:::


Building the `reprex` solves half the problems before you even ask: by isolating
the error in a five-line example, you often find the cause on your own.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Check what was generated

1. **AI makes things up.** Arguments that do not exist, functions from outdated packages, column
   names that are not in your data. Run it and check on a small subset where you know
   the right answer.
2. **AI does not know your dataset.** It does not know that VISUM's `VEHKMTRAVPRT` comes in metres,
   nor that the Comex Stat municipality code is not the IBGE one (@sec-m3-comexstat). That
   knowledge is yours, and it is what makes the result defensible.
3. **Ask for the explanation, not just the code.** The goal of the course is for you to be able to read,
   fix and technically defend what the script does.
:::

A useful prompt in our context has four parts: what you have, what you want, with which
tool and what the constraint is. For example: *"I have a data.frame with columns origin state, destination
state and TKU. I want the 10 largest interstate links by TKU, using dplyr, keeping the
column names."*
